overview: The Western Zhou established the political and philosophical foundations of Chinese civilization. Through a system of enfeoffment and the concept of the Mandate of Heaven, they created a model of legitimate rulership that endured for three millennia.

items.text: The Mandate of Heaven concept emerges, stating that Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants.
The Duke of Zhou articulates the theory of dynastic succession and the ruler's moral responsibility.
Ancestor worship becomes formalized in ritual bronze vessels and temple ceremonies.
Iron smelting appears alongside bronze working, though iron remained rare during this period.
Improved bronze casting techniques for ritual vessels, bells and weapons.
The Classic of Poetry (Shijing) compiled, containing folk songs, court hymns and eulogies from the period.
The Book of Changes (Yijing) takes shape as a divination text and philosophical work.
Bronze inscriptions become longer and more literary, recording royal deeds and land grants.
Feudal lords governed territories from walled cities, owing military service and tribute to the Zhou king.
The well-field system supposedly divided agricultural land into nine plots, with the center plot worked for the lord.
Confucius later idealized the Western Zhou as a golden age of virtue and proper ritual.
The Mandate of Heaven justified political change throughout Chinese history until 1911.
Zhou ritual codes influenced East Asian court ceremonies for centuries.

fall.text: Quanrong nomads allied with disaffected lords sacked the capital Haojing and killed King You, forcing the court to flee east.
